changes.text: Irinotecan 50 mg/m² intravenously and temozolomide 100 mg/m² by mouth are given on days 1–5 of each 21-day cycle. The national plan specifies 6 cycles unless progression, toxicity or the specialist plan changes treatment. Take temozolomide fasting, swallowed whole with water, at least one hour before irinotecan. If you vomit after temozolomide, do not take an extra dose.

required_units.text: Space for your own treatment record, questions and notes, followed by your treatment card.
Irinotecan and temozolomideNational Cancer Control Programme (NCCP) 00504

Record each cycle separately. Each medicine has its own symptom table. Mark the worst symptoms since your last review, when they occurred and what they stopped you doing. Overlapping symptoms can be recorded under more than one medicine; you do not have to identify the cause.

These are patient-language severity prompts, not a validated questionnaire or a formal Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) grading tool. Your team assigns the clinical grade. Serious symptoms override the columns: call without waiting to decide a severity level.
Use a new record sheet for each cycle or review. Copy or print another sheet when needed; the number of sheets does not prescribe the length of treatment.
Source-reconciled feasibility draft; independent clinician, pharmacy and patient review pending.
Bring this record to every treatment and review; your team confirms the dose and next appointment.
Days 1–5 · every 21 days · 6 planned cycles · copy this sheet for another cycle of the same phase.

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Call oncology immediately for fever, shaking chills, suddenly feeling unwell, unusual bleeding, new breathlessness, very little urine, severe rash or vomiting that prevents drinking. Follow your hospital’s temperature and contact instructions. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or seizures: call 112/999. Irinotecan can cause two different bowel problems. Cramping, sweating and diarrhoea during or shortly after infusion can be an acute cholinergic reaction: tell the nurse immediately; prescribed atropine may be used. Delayed diarrhoea begins more than 24 hours later and can cause dangerous dehydration or infection. Contact oncology at the first loose stool and follow the written anti-diarrhoeal and rehydration prescription. Fever, severe pain, blood, faintness, very little urine or inability to drink needs immediate assessment; never wait for a time threshold when seriously unwell. Report a new cough, breathlessness, jaundice, severe rash or marked weakness urgently.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.
Aim to shrink or control cancer and help symptoms after previous treatment. Your specialist explains the realistic benefit, uncertainty and alternatives for your particular disease.

Irinotecan blocks topoisomerase I, an enzyme involved in handling deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), the cell's genetic material. Cancer-cell division is disrupted. Blood and bowel cells are also affected. Early infusion-related bowel symptoms and later diarrhoea need different treatment plans.

What to watch forTell staff about cramping, sweating, runny eyes/nose or diarrhoea during or soon after infusion. Later watery stools require the prescribed diarrhoea plan and immediate oncology contact. Fever, dizziness, reduced urine, severe abdominal pain or inability to drink needs urgent assessment.

The body converts temozolomide into an active substance that damages deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), the cell's genetic material, interrupting cell division. Although taken as capsules, it can cause serious blood, liver and infection problems and requires the prescribed checks.

What to watch forReport fever, new cough or breathlessness, unusual bleeding, jaundice, severe rash or persistent vomiting urgently. Take capsules exactly as prescribed; do not replace a dose after vomiting. Follow the infection-prevention prescription and report any missed doses to the team.
The drawings are simplified explanations of drug action, not anatomical pictures or a prediction of response.
This shows treatment timing, not guaranteed symptom-free days. Your team confirms the active phase and dates.

Irinotecan 50 mg/m² intravenously and temozolomide 100 mg/m² by mouth are given on days 1–5 of each 21-day cycle. The national plan specifies 6 cycles unless progression, toxicity or the specialist plan changes treatment. Take temozolomide fasting, swallowed whole with water, at least one hour before irinotecan. If you vomit after temozolomide, do not take an extra dose.

This is the 50 mg/m² irinotecan, 100 mg/m² temozolomide, six-cycle Ewing regimen. Other published schedules and the vincristine-containing rhabdomyosarcoma regimen are different. Use for this diagnosis is unlicensed in Ireland. Your team must explain why it is recommended, document your consent under hospital policy and confirm acknowledgement by the hospital’s Drugs and Therapeutics Committee or equivalent.
Safety monitoring is separate from scans and tumour-response review. The exact sequence can change after toxicity or local treatment.

Irinotecan is infused over 60 minutes after the oral temozolomide dose, with prescribed anti-sickness and bowel protection. Confirm which doses are taken at home or in the unit and bring the exact capsule prescription; capsule strengths can differ.

The treatment service chooses suitable intravenous access. Report burning, pain, swelling or redness during administration immediately. Follow one written prevention, home and rescue plan. The team reconciles all steroids and interacting medicines; no generic reference is an additional prescription.

Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prevention is required with this temozolomide regimen. The prescribed medicine helps prevent an opportunistic lung infection; follow its full course and report new cough or breathlessness. Hepatitis B results may require a separate expert prevention and follow-up plan.

Sweating, cramps and early diarrhoea during or soon after infusion can be a cholinergic reaction. Tell the nurse immediately. The national regimen says atropine should not be used in patients with glaucoma. Tell the treatment team if you have glaucoma. This source does not give a fixed atropine dose.

Irinotecan can cause two different bowel problems. Cramping, sweating and diarrhoea during or shortly after infusion can be an acute cholinergic reaction: tell the nurse immediately; prescribed atropine may be used. Delayed diarrhoea begins more than 24 hours later and can cause dangerous dehydration or infection. Contact oncology at the first loose stool and follow the written anti-diarrhoeal and rehydration prescription. Fever, severe pain, blood, faintness, very little urine or inability to drink needs immediate assessment; never wait for a time threshold when seriously unwell.

If a temozolomide dose is missed, contact the treatment team for instructions. Never double a dose or restart a held course yourself. If vomiting occurs after temozolomide, do not take an extra dose. Capsules must be swallowed whole, fasting, at least one hour before irinotecan.

Discuss fertility preservation before treatment; these combinations can permanently affect fertility. Obtain a written pregnancy-prevention, contraception and breastfeeding plan covering every medicine and the longest relevant precaution period. Current product instructions differ from the older general six-month regimen paragraph. Do not assume one interval applies to everyone, and contact oncology promptly if pregnancy is possible.

Discuss low blood counts with serious infection or sepsis, anaemia and bleeding; nausea or vomiting; mouth soreness, appetite or taste changes, diarrhoea or constipation; fatigue, hair, nail and skin changes; changes in sexual wellbeing; allergic reactions and intravenous-line complications; blood clots, including clots in the legs or lungs; fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding effects; and the possibility of lasting organ injury, later cancers or death from serious treatment complications. The likelihood and severity differ between medicines, doses and people. Read this general section together with the risks of every medicine actually included in the agreed treatment phase.

Discuss realistic benefit and uncertainty, alternatives including clinical trials or symptom-focused care where appropriate, common and serious risks, lasting effects, personal priorities and the option to decline or reconsider treatment. This is the 50 mg/m² irinotecan, 100 mg/m² temozolomide, six-cycle Ewing regimen. Other published schedules and the vincristine-containing rhabdomyosarcoma regimen are different. Use for this diagnosis is unlicensed in Ireland. Your team must explain why it is recommended, document your consent under hospital policy and confirm acknowledgement by the hospital’s Drugs and Therapeutics Committee or equivalent.

Prospective interim trial evidence and retrospective studies show activity in some relapsed Ewing sarcomas. In the rEECur comparison, the irinotecan/temozolomide arm was less effective than the other then-open arms and was closed. The existence of responses does not establish superiority or an individual chance of benefit.

The rEECur figures are from an interim conference report, not a completed full-paper comparison. Retrospective series are subject to selection bias; the adult-containing Palmerini series used irinotecan 40 mg/m², not this national 50 mg/m² schedule. Disease control includes stable disease and must not be labelled response.

changes.text: There are 14 alternating administrations, planned every 14 days after recovery, not 14 pairs. Ifosfamide and etoposide are given on days 1–5 in cycles 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 and 13. Vincristine, doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide are given on day 1 in cycles 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10. Cycles 12 and 14 contain vincristine and cyclophosphamide with no doxorubicin; dactinomycin may be added only if the consultant selects it. Surgery, radiotherapy, toxicity or delayed recovery may change the sequence or dates.

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Call oncology immediately for fever, shaking chills, suddenly feeling unwell, unusual bleeding, new breathlessness, very little urine, severe rash or vomiting that prevents drinking. Follow your hospital’s temperature and contact instructions. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or seizures: call 112/999. Confusion or unusual drowsiness during ifosfamide, blood in urine, reduced urine, severe constipation, new weakness or heart symptoms needs urgent assessment. Doxorubicin can colour urine red for one or two days; do not dismiss painful urination, clots or suspected blood as harmless colour.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.
Treat cancer throughout the body as part of a specialist plan that also addresses local tumour control. The intended benefit depends on the exact tumour, disease extent and treatment aim.

The liver activates ifosfamide into substances that damage deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), the cell's genetic material. Some breakdown products can injure the urinary tract. Mesna and prescribed fluids reduce bladder injury, but do not remove kidney, brain or other chemotherapy risks.

What to watch forReport confusion, unusual sleepiness, hallucinations, marked weakness or seizures immediately. Blood or pain when passing urine, reduced urine, fever or new breathing problems needs urgent review. Continue prescribed mesna and hydration until the team confirms completion.

Etoposide interferes with topoisomerase II, an enzyme that manages breaks in deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), the cell's genetic material. Damaged cancer cells cannot divide normally. Blood production and other healthy tissues can also be affected.

What to watch forTell the nurse immediately about dizziness, flushing, rash, chest tightness, breathlessness, faintness or infusion-site pain. Contact oncology promptly for fever, bleeding, severe mouth symptoms or a blistering rash.

Vincristine interferes with microtubules, structures needed for cells to divide and for nerves to work normally. This helps explain numbness, weakness and bowel slowing. It is given only into a vein by trained staff; administration into spinal fluid can be fatal.

What to watch forReport new numbness, weakness, difficulty walking, jaw pain or hearing/vision changes before another dose. Constipation with pain, vomiting or abdominal swelling, difficulty passing urine, confusion or seizures needs urgent advice. Report infusion-site pain immediately.

Doxorubicin interferes with deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), the cell's genetic material, and the enzymes that manage it. Cancer cells can be damaged, but blood production, the mouth and the heart can also be affected. Previous anthracycline treatment contributes to the heart-risk assessment.

What to watch forReport fever, new breathlessness, chest symptoms or palpitations urgently. Tell staff immediately about infusion-site burning or pain. Temporary red urine may reflect the medicine's colour, but visible blood, clots, painful urination or persistent red urine needs assessment.

Cyclophosphamide is activated into substances that damage deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), the cell's genetic material. Blood and reproductive cells can also be affected. Urinary breakdown products can injure the bladder, so the prescribed fluid and any mesna plan must be followed.

What to watch forReport blood or pain when passing urine, reduced urine, fever, new breathlessness, chest symptoms, confusion or severe weakness urgently. Follow the individual fluid plan; do not force large fluid volumes if you have a fluid restriction.

This medicine is optional in the final two even-numbered administrations and is included in your consent only if selected. Dactinomycin binds to deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), the cell's genetic material, and disrupts production of ribonucleic acid (RNA), which carries instructions for cell activity. Cancer cells and healthy blood, mouth, gut and liver tissues can be affected.

What to watch forReport fever, bleeding, severe mouth sores or diarrhoea, jaundice, increasing abdominal pain/swelling or rapid weight gain urgently. Tell staff immediately about infusion-site pain or burning. Report a new painful rash, especially in a previously irradiated area.

There are 14 alternating administrations, planned every 14 days after recovery, not 14 pairs. Ifosfamide and etoposide are given on days 1–5 in cycles 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 and 13. Vincristine, doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide are given on day 1 in cycles 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10. During ifosfamide/etoposide cycles, each medicine is infused over 60 minutes on each of days 1–5. During the alternating day-1 cycles, vincristine is given by an intravenous minibag over 15 minutes, conventional doxorubicin by slow intravenous bolus, and cyclophosphamide over 30 minutes. Optional final-phase dactinomycin is given by trained staff. Mesna, fluids, tests and observation add substantially to attendance time.

If a port or central catheter is used, agree dressing, flushing, infection precautions and eventual removal arrangements. Do not alter infusion or mesna-pump settings yourself.

Follow one written prevention, home and rescue plan. The team reconciles all steroids and interacting medicines; no generic reference is an additional prescription.

Ifosfamide cycles: mesna 360 mg/m² intravenously before each dose and at 4 and 8 hours from the START of that dose. It binds bladder-damaging metabolites; it does not prevent every kidney or neurological effect.

Hospital-prescribed fluids support urine flow and clearance. The team adjusts them to urine output, blood tests, weight and heart/kidney status; continue the prescribed protection after chemotherapy finishes. Follow individual home fluid advice.

Required after every administration. After ifosfamide/etoposide: daily injections on days 8–13 (source 0.5 million units/kg, maximum 48 million units/day for primary prevention). After vincristine/cyclophosphamide-containing treatment: pegylated injection 24–48 hours later. These support recovery of infection-fighting cells; fever still needs urgent assessment.

Use the prescribed mouth-care and constipation-prevention plan. Vincristine slows bowel movement through nerve effects; report painful constipation, vomiting or abdominal swelling promptly. Mouth care helps detect and manage damaged lining before drinking becomes difficult.

If pelvic radiotherapy is planned, additional mesna is prescribed with cyclophosphamide: 240 mg/m² intravenously before it, then 240 mg/m² intravenously or 480 mg/m² orally 4 and 8 hours from its start. Doxorubicin interruption depends on the radiation field; it is not reintroduced until at least three weeks after radiation ends. Confirm actual dates with both teams.

Discuss fertility preservation before treatment; these combinations can permanently affect fertility. Obtain a written pregnancy-prevention, contraception and breastfeeding plan covering every medicine and the longest relevant precaution period. Current product instructions differ from the older general six-month regimen paragraph. Do not assume one interval applies to everyone, and contact oncology promptly if pregnancy is possible.

For Ewing sarcoma, systemic chemotherapy is combined with surgery and/or radiotherapy for local tumour control. For rhabdomyosarcoma, the specialist combines systemic and local treatment according to site, risk and feasibility. These decisions require the relevant multidisciplinary team; Ewing trial percentages cannot be used as estimates for the other listed tumour types. Rehabilitation, symptom control and psychological support can accompany cancer treatment.

There are 14 alternating administrations, planned every 14 days after recovery, not 14 pairs. Ifosfamide and etoposide are given on days 1–5 in cycles 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 and 13. Vincristine, doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide are given on day 1 in cycles 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10. Cycles 12 and 14 contain vincristine and cyclophosphamide with no doxorubicin; dactinomycin may be added only if the consultant selects it. Surgery, radiotherapy, toxicity or delayed recovery may change the sequence or dates.
The named monitoring cards describe each test’s purpose and timing.
Confirm which samples and reviews are due, where they happen and who authorises the next dose.
Normal blood tests do not show that cancer is responding. The specialist sets separate scan, symptom and local-treatment reviews.
Use the medicine-specific support instructions and actual prescription.
The support section explains why each protective measure is used. Confirm the dose, start day and finish day on your own prescription; do not combine alternative reference prescriptions.
Report new or worsening symptoms promptly.

Call oncology immediately for fever, shaking chills, suddenly feeling unwell, unusual bleeding, new breathlessness, very little urine, severe rash or vomiting that prevents drinking. Follow your hospital’s temperature and contact instructions. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or seizures: call 112/999. Confusion or unusual drowsiness during ifosfamide, blood in urine, reduced urine, severe constipation, new weakness or heart symptoms needs urgent assessment. Doxorubicin can colour urine red for one or two days; do not dismiss painful urination, clots or suspected blood as harmless colour.
Tell the nurse immediately about flushing, rash, chills, breathlessness, faintness or pain/swelling at the infusion site.
Keep verified daytime and out-of-hours oncology numbers with your treatment card. The quick response code website is information, not an emergency service.
Read the general chemotherapy risks together with each medicine-specific section.

Discuss low blood counts with serious infection or sepsis, anaemia and bleeding; nausea or vomiting; mouth soreness, appetite or taste changes, diarrhoea or constipation; fatigue, hair, nail and skin changes; changes in sexual wellbeing; allergic reactions and intravenous-line complications; blood clots, including clots in the legs or lungs; fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding effects; and the possibility of lasting organ injury, later cancers or death from serious treatment complications. The likelihood and severity differ between medicines, doses and people. Read this general section together with the risks of every medicine actually included in the agreed treatment phase.

Discuss realistic benefit and uncertainty, alternatives including clinical trials or symptom-focused care where appropriate, common and serious risks, lasting effects, personal priorities and the option to decline or reconsider treatment. This is the 14-day national schedule for adolescents and young adults. The regimen guidance does not specify a numerical age or fitness-score limit. The treatment starts with ifosfamide/etoposide. The final two even-numbered administrations omit doxorubicin, and dactinomycin remains optional. Trial schedules and other age-group protocols are not interchangeable.

In a randomised trial of predominantly children and adolescents with localised Ewing sarcoma, giving alternating chemotherapy every two weeks improved event-free survival compared with every three weeks. Longer follow-up of the same study supported sustained benefit. This evidence informs interval choice but does not make the individual national calendars identical to the study.

The trial population was mostly young and had localised Ewing sarcoma. It began with vincristine/doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide, whereas these national schedules begin with ifosfamide/etoposide; some doses and recovery thresholds also differ. Do not transfer Ewing outcomes to rhabdomyosarcoma, desmoplastic tumours, metastatic disease or every adult. Long-term follow-up is the same cohort, not an independent trial.

Treat cancer throughout the body as part of a specialist plan that also addresses local tumour control. The intended benefit depends on the exact tumour, disease extent and treatment aim. For Ewing sarcoma, systemic chemotherapy is combined with surgery and/or radiotherapy for local tumour control. For rhabdomyosarcoma, the specialist combines systemic and local treatment according to site, risk and feasibility. These decisions require the relevant multidisciplinary team; Ewing trial percentages cannot be used as estimates for the other listed tumour types. Rehabilitation, symptom control and psychological support can accompany cancer treatment.
No. Blood counts, organ function and symptoms can make a delay or dose change safer. Your team decides whether and when to give the next dose.
Use your verified oncology daytime or out-of-hours number. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Severe symptoms require 112/999.
Only after the treating team confirms the new prescription. A normal test or recovered symptom does not erase previous severe toxicity or a permanent-stop decision.

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Call oncology immediately for fever, shaking chills, suddenly feeling unwell, unusual bleeding, new breathlessness, very little urine, severe rash or vomiting that prevents drinking. Follow your hospital’s temperature and contact instructions. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or seizures: call 112/999. Confusion or unusual drowsiness during ifosfamide, blood in urine, reduced urine, severe constipation, new weakness or heart symptoms needs urgent assessment. Doxorubicin can colour urine red for one or two days; do not dismiss painful urination, clots or suspected blood as harmless colour.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.
Treat cancer throughout the body as part of a specialist plan that also addresses local tumour control. The intended benefit depends on the exact tumour, disease extent and treatment aim.

The liver activates ifosfamide into substances that damage deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), the cell's genetic material. Some breakdown products can injure the urinary tract. Mesna and prescribed fluids reduce bladder injury, but do not remove kidney, brain or other chemotherapy risks.

What to watch forReport confusion, unusual sleepiness, hallucinations, marked weakness or seizures immediately. Blood or pain when passing urine, reduced urine, fever or new breathing problems needs urgent review. Continue prescribed mesna and hydration until the team confirms completion.

Etoposide interferes with topoisomerase II, an enzyme that manages breaks in deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), the cell's genetic material. Damaged cancer cells cannot divide normally. Blood production and other healthy tissues can also be affected.

What to watch forTell the nurse immediately about dizziness, flushing, rash, chest tightness, breathlessness, faintness or infusion-site pain. Contact oncology promptly for fever, bleeding, severe mouth symptoms or a blistering rash.

Vincristine interferes with microtubules, structures needed for cells to divide and for nerves to work normally. This helps explain numbness, weakness and bowel slowing. It is given only into a vein by trained staff; administration into spinal fluid can be fatal.

What to watch forReport new numbness, weakness, difficulty walking, jaw pain or hearing/vision changes before another dose. Constipation with pain, vomiting or abdominal swelling, difficulty passing urine, confusion or seizures needs urgent advice. Report infusion-site pain immediately.

Doxorubicin interferes with deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), the cell's genetic material, and the enzymes that manage it. Cancer cells can be damaged, but blood production, the mouth and the heart can also be affected. Previous anthracycline treatment contributes to the heart-risk assessment.

What to watch forReport fever, new breathlessness, chest symptoms or palpitations urgently. Tell staff immediately about infusion-site burning or pain. Temporary red urine may reflect the medicine's colour, but visible blood, clots, painful urination or persistent red urine needs assessment.

Cyclophosphamide is activated into substances that damage deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), the cell's genetic material. Blood and reproductive cells can also be affected. Urinary breakdown products can injure the bladder, so the prescribed fluid and any mesna plan must be followed.

What to watch forReport blood or pain when passing urine, reduced urine, fever, new breathlessness, chest symptoms, confusion or severe weakness urgently. Follow the individual fluid plan; do not force large fluid volumes if you have a fluid restriction.

This medicine is optional in the final two even-numbered administrations and is included in your consent only if selected. Dactinomycin binds to deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), the cell's genetic material, and disrupts production of ribonucleic acid (RNA), which carries instructions for cell activity. Cancer cells and healthy blood, mouth, gut and liver tissues can be affected.

What to watch forReport fever, bleeding, severe mouth sores or diarrhoea, jaundice, increasing abdominal pain/swelling or rapid weight gain urgently. Tell staff immediately about infusion-site pain or burning. Report a new painful rash, especially in a previously irradiated area.

There are 14 alternating administrations, planned every 21 days after recovery, not 14 pairs. Ifosfamide and etoposide are given on days 1–5 in cycles 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 and 13. Vincristine, doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide are given on day 1 in cycles 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10. Cycles 12 and 14 contain vincristine and cyclophosphamide with no doxorubicin; dactinomycin may be added only if the consultant selects it. Surgery, radiotherapy, toxicity or delayed recovery may change the sequence or dates. Confirm the phase and actual prescribed treatment days before every administration.
Agree the arrangements with your oncology team.

Confirm the current numbered administration and which drugs it contains. Review constipation prevention, mouth care, medicines and infection contacts. If pelvic radiotherapy is planned, the team prescribes additional mesna with cyclophosphamide. Confirm the timing of chemotherapy around radiation.

During ifosfamide/etoposide cycles, each medicine is infused over 60 minutes on each of days 1–5. During the alternating day-1 cycles, vincristine is given by an intravenous minibag over 15 minutes, conventional doxorubicin by slow intravenous bolus, and cyclophosphamide over 30 minutes. Optional final-phase dactinomycin is given by trained staff. Mesna, fluids, tests and observation add substantially to attendance time.

The treatment service chooses suitable intravenous access. Report burning, pain, swelling or redness during administration immediately. If a port or central catheter is used, agree dressing, flushing, infection precautions and eventual removal arrangements. Do not alter infusion or mesna-pump settings yourself.
Check the support section and your prescription for current protective medicines, timing and contact instructions.
Confirm the next treatment, tests and any scan before leaving.
Follow one written prevention, home and rescue plan. The team reconciles all steroids and interacting medicines; no generic reference is an additional prescription.

Ifosfamide cycles: mesna 360 mg/m² intravenously before each dose and at 4 and 8 hours from the START of that dose. It binds bladder-damaging metabolites; it does not prevent every kidney or neurological effect.

Hospital-prescribed fluids support urine flow and clearance. The team adjusts them to urine output, blood tests, weight and heart/kidney status; continue the prescribed protection after chemotherapy finishes. Follow individual home fluid advice.

Required after every administration. The local prescription selects the standard or pegylated product and timing; do not copy the two-week regimen’s days 8–13 schedule. These support recovery of infection-fighting cells; fever still needs urgent assessment.

Use the prescribed mouth-care and constipation-prevention plan. Vincristine slows bowel movement through nerve effects; report painful constipation, vomiting or abdominal swelling promptly. Mouth care helps detect and manage damaged lining before drinking becomes difficult.

If pelvic radiotherapy is planned, additional mesna is prescribed with cyclophosphamide: 240 mg/m² intravenously before it, then 240 mg/m² intravenously or 480 mg/m² orally 4 and 8 hours from its start. Doxorubicin interruption depends on the radiation field; it is not reintroduced until at least three weeks after radiation ends. Confirm actual dates with both teams.

Discuss fertility preservation before treatment; these combinations can permanently affect fertility. Obtain a written pregnancy-prevention, contraception and breastfeeding plan covering every medicine and the longest relevant precaution period. Current product instructions differ from the older general six-month regimen paragraph. Do not assume one interval applies to everyone, and contact oncology promptly if pregnancy is possible.

For Ewing sarcoma, systemic chemotherapy is combined with surgery and/or radiotherapy for local tumour control. For rhabdomyosarcoma, the specialist combines systemic and local treatment according to site, risk and feasibility. These decisions require the relevant multidisciplinary team; Ewing trial percentages cannot be used as estimates for the other listed tumour types. Rehabilitation, symptom control and psychological support can accompany cancer treatment.

There are 14 alternating administrations, planned every 21 days after recovery, not 14 pairs. Ifosfamide and etoposide are given on days 1–5 in cycles 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 and 13. Vincristine, doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide are given on day 1 in cycles 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10. Cycles 12 and 14 contain vincristine and cyclophosphamide with no doxorubicin; dactinomycin may be added only if the consultant selects it. Surgery, radiotherapy, toxicity or delayed recovery may change the sequence or dates.

Normal blood tests do not show that cancer is responding. The specialist sets separate scan, symptom and local-treatment reviews.
Use the medicine-specific support instructions and actual prescription.
The support section explains why each protective measure is used. Confirm the dose, start day and finish day on your own prescription; do not combine alternative reference prescriptions.
Report new or worsening symptoms promptly.

Call oncology immediately for fever, shaking chills, suddenly feeling unwell, unusual bleeding, new breathlessness, very little urine, severe rash or vomiting that prevents drinking. Follow your hospital’s temperature and contact instructions. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or seizures: call 112/999. Confusion or unusual drowsiness during ifosfamide, blood in urine, reduced urine, severe constipation, new weakness or heart symptoms needs urgent assessment. Doxorubicin can colour urine red for one or two days; do not dismiss painful urination, clots or suspected blood as harmless colour.
Tell the nurse immediately about flushing, rash, chills, breathlessness, faintness or pain/swelling at the infusion site.
Keep verified daytime and out-of-hours oncology numbers with your treatment card. The quick response code website is information, not an emergency service.
Read the general chemotherapy risks together with each medicine-specific section.

Discuss low blood counts with serious infection or sepsis, anaemia and bleeding; nausea or vomiting; mouth soreness, appetite or taste changes, diarrhoea or constipation; fatigue, hair, nail and skin changes; changes in sexual wellbeing; allergic reactions and intravenous-line complications; blood clots, including clots in the legs or lungs; fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding effects; and the possibility of lasting organ injury, later cancers or death from serious treatment complications. The likelihood and severity differ between medicines, doses and people. Read this general section together with the risks of every medicine actually included in the agreed treatment phase.

Discuss realistic benefit and uncertainty, alternatives including clinical trials or symptom-focused care where appropriate, common and serious risks, lasting effects, personal priorities and the option to decline or reconsider treatment. This is the 21-day national schedule for adults. The regimen guidance does not specify a numerical age or fitness-score limit. The treatment starts with ifosfamide/etoposide. The final two even-numbered administrations omit doxorubicin, and dactinomycin remains optional. Trial schedules and other age-group protocols are not interchangeable.

In a randomised trial of predominantly children and adolescents with localised Ewing sarcoma, giving alternating chemotherapy every two weeks improved event-free survival compared with every three weeks. Longer follow-up of the same study supported sustained benefit. This evidence informs interval choice but does not make the individual national calendars identical to the study.

The trial population was mostly young and had localised Ewing sarcoma. It began with vincristine/doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide, whereas these national schedules begin with ifosfamide/etoposide; some doses and recovery thresholds also differ. Do not transfer Ewing outcomes to rhabdomyosarcoma, desmoplastic tumours, metastatic disease or every adult. Long-term follow-up is the same cohort, not an independent trial.

For Ewing sarcoma, systemic chemotherapy is combined with surgery and/or radiotherapy for local tumour control. For rhabdomyosarcoma, the specialist combines systemic and local treatment according to site, risk and feasibility. These decisions require the relevant multidisciplinary team; Ewing trial percentages cannot be used as estimates for the other listed tumour types. Rehabilitation, symptom control and psychological support can accompany cancer treatment.
No. Blood counts, organ function and symptoms can make a delay or dose change safer. Your team decides whether and when to give the next dose.
Use your verified oncology daytime or out-of-hours number. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Severe symptoms require 112/999.
Only after the treating team confirms the new prescription. A normal test or recovered symptom does not erase previous severe toxicity or a permanent-stop decision.

changes.text: Treat rhabdomyosarcoma throughout the body as part of an individual specialist plan that also addresses local tumour control. The team explains why this combination is selected for your risk group and priorities.

changes.reason: Complete repeated clinical statement retained verbatim in an earlier explanation
changes.text: Vincristine 1.5 mg/m², maximum 2 mg, is given by an intravenous minibag over 15 minutes. Dactinomycin 1.5 mg/m², maximum 2 mg, and doxorubicin 30 mg/m² on each of days 1 and 2 are administered by trained staff as intravenous boluses. Ifosfamide 3000 mg/m² on each of days 1 and 2 is infused over three hours. Mesna, fluids, safety review and observation add to the attendance or admission time.

changes.reason: Complete repeated clinical statement retained verbatim in an earlier explanation
changes.text: Rhabdomyosarcoma treatment combines systemic therapy with local treatment tailored to tumour site, risk and feasible surgery and/or radiotherapy. The multidisciplinary team coordinates these components. The choice of an additional anthracycline requires a separate benefit–risk discussion because the randomised evidence in high-risk non-metastatic disease did not demonstrate a significant event-free-survival benefit from adding doxorubicin.

changes.text: Discuss fertility preservation before treatment; these combinations can permanently affect fertility. Obtain a written pregnancy-prevention, contraception and breastfeeding plan covering every medicine and the longest relevant precaution period. Current product instructions differ from the older general six-month regimen paragraph. Do not assume one interval applies to everyone, and contact oncology promptly if pregnancy is possible.

New confusion, unusual drowsiness or seizures, blood in urine, very little urine, severe constipation, new weakness or breathlessness requires urgent assessment. Report infusion-site burning immediately.

changes.text: Nine cycles are planned every 21 days. In cycles 1–2, vincristine is given on days 1, 8 and 15; doxorubicin on days 1 and 2; dactinomycin on day 1; and ifosfamide on days 1 and 2. In cycles 3–4, vincristine is given only on day 1, with the other three drugs on the same days as before. In cycles 5–9, doxorubicin is omitted; day-1 vincristine/dactinomycin and day-1/2 ifosfamide continue. Use the correct phase chart for your actual cycle.

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Call oncology immediately for fever, shaking chills, suddenly feeling unwell, unusual bleeding, new breathlessness, very little urine, severe rash or vomiting that prevents drinking. Follow your hospital’s temperature and contact instructions. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or seizures: call 112/999. New confusion, unusual drowsiness or seizures, blood in urine, very little urine, severe constipation, new weakness or breathlessness requires urgent assessment. Report infusion-site burning immediately.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.

Treat rhabdomyosarcoma throughout the body as part of an individual specialist plan that also addresses local tumour control. The team explains why this combination is selected for your risk group and priorities.

The liver activates ifosfamide into substances that damage deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), the cell's genetic material. Some breakdown products can injure the urinary tract. Mesna and prescribed fluids reduce bladder injury, but do not remove kidney, brain or other chemotherapy risks.

What to watch forReport confusion, unusual sleepiness, hallucinations, marked weakness or seizures immediately. Blood or pain when passing urine, reduced urine, fever or new breathing problems needs urgent review. Continue prescribed mesna and hydration until the team confirms completion.

Vincristine interferes with microtubules, structures needed for cells to divide and for nerves to work normally. This helps explain numbness, weakness and bowel slowing. It is given only into a vein by trained staff; administration into spinal fluid can be fatal.

What to watch forReport new numbness, weakness, difficulty walking, jaw pain or hearing/vision changes before another dose. Constipation with pain, vomiting or abdominal swelling, difficulty passing urine, confusion or seizures needs urgent advice. Report infusion-site pain immediately.

Dactinomycin binds to deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), the cell's genetic material, and disrupts production of ribonucleic acid (RNA), which carries instructions for cell activity. Cancer cells and healthy blood, mouth, gut and liver tissues can be affected.

What to watch forReport fever, bleeding, severe mouth sores or diarrhoea, jaundice, increasing abdominal pain/swelling or rapid weight gain urgently. Tell staff immediately about infusion-site pain or burning. Report a new painful rash, especially in a previously irradiated area.

Doxorubicin interferes with deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), the cell's genetic material, and the enzymes that manage it. Cancer cells can be damaged, but blood production, the mouth and the heart can also be affected. Previous anthracycline treatment contributes to the heart-risk assessment.

What to watch forReport fever, new breathlessness, chest symptoms or palpitations urgently. Tell staff immediately about infusion-site burning or pain. Temporary red urine may reflect the medicine's colour, but visible blood, clots, painful urination or persistent red urine needs assessment.

Nine cycles are planned every 21 days. In cycles 1–2, vincristine is given on days 1, 8 and 15; doxorubicin on days 1 and 2; dactinomycin on day 1; and ifosfamide on days 1 and 2. In cycles 3–4, vincristine is given only on day 1, with the other three drugs on the same days as before. In cycles 5–9, doxorubicin is omitted; day-1 vincristine/dactinomycin and day-1/2 ifosfamide continue. Use the correct phase chart for your actual cycle. Confirm the phase and actual prescribed treatment days before every administration.
Agree the arrangements with your oncology team.

Confirm whether this is cycle 1–2, 3–4 or 5–9, and which vincristine appointments and doxorubicin doses apply. Check the full mesna/hydration prescription and the growth-factor calendar. Ask about individual infection prevention, bowel support and medicines that may interact.

Vincristine 1.5 mg/m², maximum 2 mg, is given by an intravenous minibag over 15 minutes. Dactinomycin 1.5 mg/m², maximum 2 mg, and doxorubicin 30 mg/m² on each of days 1 and 2 are administered by trained staff as intravenous boluses. Ifosfamide 3000 mg/m² on each of days 1 and 2 is infused over three hours. Mesna, fluids, safety review and observation add to the attendance or admission time.

The treatment service chooses suitable intravenous access. Report burning, pain, swelling or redness during administration immediately. If a port or central catheter is used, agree dressing, flushing, infection precautions and eventual removal arrangements. Do not alter infusion or mesna-pump settings yourself.
Check the support section and your prescription for current protective medicines, timing and contact instructions.
Confirm the next treatment, tests and any scan before leaving.
Follow one written prevention, home and rescue plan. The team reconciles all steroids and interacting medicines; no generic reference is an additional prescription.

On each of days 1 and 2, mesna 900 mg/m² intravenously over ten minutes immediately before ifosfamide, then 3000 mg/m² continuously over 24 hours starting with ifosfamide. It binds bladder-damaging metabolites; kidney and brain monitoring are still required.

Hospital-prescribed fluids support urine flow and clearance. The team adjusts them to urine output, blood tests, weight and heart/kidney status; continue the prescribed protection after chemotherapy finishes. Follow individual home fluid advice.

Cycles 1–2: daily injections on days 4–7 and 9–11 at the prescribed 5 micrograms/kg. Cycles 3–9: pegylated growth factor may be considered from day 4. These support marrow recovery; the later plan is not automatically the same as the early plan.

Use the prescribed mouth-care and constipation-prevention plan. Vincristine slows bowel movement through nerve effects; report painful constipation, vomiting or abdominal swelling promptly. Mouth care helps detect and manage damaged lining before drinking becomes difficult.

The team considers Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and antifungal prevention, and any tumour-lysis precautions. These are individual decisions here. Azole antifungals can increase vincristine toxicity; pharmacy must reconcile the plan.

Discuss fertility preservation before treatment; these combinations can permanently affect fertility. Obtain a written pregnancy-prevention, contraception and breastfeeding plan covering every medicine and the longest relevant precaution period. Current product instructions differ from the older general six-month regimen paragraph. Do not assume one interval applies to everyone, and contact oncology promptly if pregnancy is possible.

The multidisciplinary team coordinates these components. The choice of an additional anthracycline requires a separate benefit–risk discussion because the randomised evidence in high-risk non-metastatic disease did not demonstrate a significant event-free-survival benefit from adding doxorubicin.

Discuss low blood counts with serious infection or sepsis, anaemia and bleeding; nausea or vomiting; mouth soreness, appetite or taste changes, diarrhoea or constipation; fatigue, hair, nail and skin changes; changes in sexual wellbeing; allergic reactions and intravenous-line complications; blood clots, including clots in the legs or lungs; fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding effects; and the possibility of lasting organ injury, later cancers or death from serious treatment complications. The likelihood and severity differ between medicines, doses and people. Read this general section together with the risks of every medicine actually included in the agreed treatment phase.

Discuss realistic benefit and uncertainty, alternatives including clinical trials or symptom-focused care where appropriate, common and serious risks, lasting effects, personal priorities and the option to decline or reconsider treatment. This is the nine-cycle regimen for high-risk or very-high-risk rhabdomyosarcoma under age 40, with performance status 0–2. It is not one unchanged calendar repeated nine times. Follow the prescribed mesna timing and the growth-factor plan for your current treatment phase; the growth-factor plan differs between earlier and later phases. Your team will explain the role of each medicine and check its licensing for your treatment.

A randomised trial in high-risk non-metastatic rhabdomyosarcoma compared the three-drug backbone with the addition of doxorubicin during the first four cycles. It did not show a statistically significant improvement in event-free survival, and serious infections were more common with doxorubicin. Treatment selection therefore needs an individual explanation, not a claim of established extra benefit for everyone.

The trial enrolled patients older than six months and younger than 21 years with non-metastatic disease; it does not directly establish benefit across the national under-40 or very-high-risk population. The trial used a four-hour doxorubicin infusion rather than the national bolus instruction. Do not claim superiority or transfer the trial outcome to every patient.

previous_short_page.text: Randomised vincristine/irinotecan with or without temozolomide in relapsed rhabdomyosarcoma A randomised study found a higher observed response and longer overall survival with the three-drug combination than with vincristine/irinotecan alone, but the primary response comparison did not meet conventional statistical significance and severe adverse events were more frequent. Most participants were children; adult-specific benefit cannot be assumed. The primary response endpoint had P=0.09; progression-free survival also did not reach conventional significance. The overall-survival result is a separate endpoint. The trial treated until progression or unacceptable toxicity, whereas the national schedule specifies 12 cycles. Mixed ages do not establish a separate adult estimate.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.
Aim to shrink or control cancer and help symptoms after previous treatment. Your specialist explains the realistic benefit, uncertainty and alternatives for your particular disease.

Vincristine interferes with microtubules, structures needed for cells to divide and for nerves to work normally. This helps explain numbness, weakness and bowel slowing. It is given only into a vein by trained staff; administration into spinal fluid can be fatal.

What to watch forReport new numbness, weakness, difficulty walking, jaw pain or hearing/vision changes before another dose. Constipation with pain, vomiting or abdominal swelling, difficulty passing urine, confusion or seizures needs urgent advice. Report infusion-site pain immediately.

Irinotecan blocks topoisomerase I, an enzyme involved in handling deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), the cell's genetic material. Cancer-cell division is disrupted. Blood and bowel cells are also affected. Early infusion-related bowel symptoms and later diarrhoea need different treatment plans.

What to watch forTell staff about cramping, sweating, runny eyes/nose or diarrhoea during or soon after infusion. Later watery stools require the prescribed diarrhoea plan and immediate oncology contact. Fever, dizziness, reduced urine, severe abdominal pain or inability to drink needs urgent assessment.

The body converts temozolomide into an active substance that damages deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), the cell's genetic material, interrupting cell division. Although taken as capsules, it can cause serious blood, liver and infection problems and requires the prescribed checks.

What to watch forReport fever, new cough or breathlessness, unusual bleeding, jaundice, severe rash or persistent vomiting urgently. Take capsules exactly as prescribed; do not replace a dose after vomiting. Follow the infection-prevention prescription and report any missed doses to the team.
The drawings are simplified explanations of drug action, not anatomical pictures or a prediction of response.
This shows treatment timing, not guaranteed symptom-free days. Your team confirms the active phase and dates.

Irinotecan 50 mg/m² is given intravenously on days 1–5 of each 21-day cycle. Temozolomide is taken by mouth on days 1–5: 125 mg/m² in cycle 1. Only the treating team may select 150 mg/m² from cycle 2 after toxicity review. Vincristine 1.5 mg/m², maximum 2 mg, is given on days 1 and 8. The national plan specifies 12 cycles unless progression, toxicity or the specialist plan changes treatment. Take temozolomide fasting, swallowed whole with water, at least one hour before irinotecan. If you vomit after temozolomide, do not take an extra dose.

This page describes adult treatment. The national regimen guidance also covers a wider age range and uses age-specific fitness criteria. Children need assessment and treatment through the appropriate specialist service. Any increase or reduction in temozolomide depends on the doses you have already received and your side effects, including previous problems that have since improved. Use for this diagnosis is unlicensed in Ireland. Your team must explain why it is recommended, document your consent under hospital policy and confirm acknowledgement by the hospital’s Drugs and Therapeutics Committee or equivalent.
Safety monitoring is separate from scans and tumour-response review. The exact sequence can change after toxicity or local treatment.

Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prevention is required with this temozolomide regimen. The prescribed medicine helps prevent an opportunistic lung infection; follow its full course and report new cough or breathlessness. The national regimen says atropine should not be used in patients with glaucoma. Tell the treatment team if you have glaucoma. Constipation prevention is recommended because vincristine slows the bowel. Antifungal prophylaxis may be considered, but interacting azoles can increase nerve and bowel toxicity and require pharmacy review.
